name: Platonism
era: From about 387 BCE, and read ever since
line: Question what you think you know, and turn towards what is good.

quote.text: The life which is unexamined is not worth living.

quotes.text: Wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.
The beginning is the most important part of the work.
No evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.
The safest general characterization of the European philosophical tradition is that it consists of a series of footnotes to Plato.
I neither know nor think that I know.

words.meaning: Form; the look of a thing
words.usage: What all beautiful things share, which is not itself any one of them. Plato also uses the word idea.

words.meaning: Form; what is seen by the mind
words.usage: Not a thought in someone’s head. For Plato an idea is more real than the things that copy it.
The highest Form, which the Republic compares to the sun. It makes everything else knowable and worth having.
Beauty and nobility in one word. A fine deed is kalon as much as a fine face.
What makes a living thing alive, and in people the seat of thought and character. Plato argues it is immortal.
To know something is to be able to give a logos of it: to say what it is and why.
Reasoning by question and answer between people who want the truth more than they want to win.
The method of Socrates. He asks for a definition, draws out what follows from it, and shows that it contradicts something else you believe.
Literally no way through. Many dialogues end here. It is counted as progress, since now you know that you do not know.
The teaching that learning is remembering what the soul knew before birth. In the Meno a slave boy works out a geometry problem from questions alone.
What most of us have most of the time. It may be true, but it cannot explain itself.
Belief that is tied down by reasons and so does not run away.
The power that grasps the Forms directly. The highest part of the soul.
The top of the divided line: thought that rises to first principles without leaning on images.
The reasoning of mathematics, which starts from assumptions and uses diagrams.
Being good at being what you are. Socrates suspected that all the virtues are one, and that it is a kind of knowledge.
The virtue of the reasoning part. Philosophy is the love of it, which admits to not yet having it.
The virtue of the spirited part: holding to what reason says is and is not to be feared.
Self-command, and agreement within the soul about which part should lead.
In the Republic, each part of the soul and each class in the city doing its own work and not meddling with the others.
The part of the soul that feels anger, pride and shame. A natural ally of reason, if well trained.
The desiring part: hunger, thirst, sex and the love of money. The largest part, and the hardest to rule.
Desire for the beautiful. In the Symposium it is the force that can carry a person all the way to the Form of Beauty.
What poets and painters do, and what things do to Forms. Plato distrusted art for being a copy of a copy.
The relation of a thing to its Form: a beautiful thing shares in Beauty. Plato knew the idea was hard to make precise.
The maker in the Timaeus, who shapes the world out of disorder by looking to the Forms.
The universe seen as a beautiful arrangement. The same word means ornament.
The forming of a whole person. In the cave image it is the turning round of the soul.

words.meaning: Constitution; the ordering of a city
words.usage: The Greek title of the Republic. It applies equally to a city and to a soul.
A grove outside the walls of Athens sacred to the hero Akademos, where Plato taught. Every later academy is named after it.

practices.name: A proof before breakfast
practices.instructions: Take paper, a pencil, a straight edge and something to draw a circle with. Work one geometrical problem by hand. Begin with the one from the Meno: draw a square, then find the square with exactly twice its area. Do not look up the answer. Struggle with it, then check. Mark the moment when you see it, not just believe it.
practices.why: In Plato’s Meno, Socrates leads a slave boy to discover the doubled square by questions alone. The Academy’s motto, let no one ignorant of geometry enter, shows how highly he prized this.
variations: Try a different proof with a friend.
Draw the problem on a wall.
Prove it two ways.

practices.name: What is it?
practices.instructions: Choose one word you rely on: courage, friendship, fairness, success. Write your best one-sentence definition. Now attack it as Socrates would. Find a case that fits the definition but is plainly not the thing, or a clear case of the thing that the definition leaves out. Revise. Repeat twice. Write your best result and what you still do not know.
practices.why: The Socratic question what is it? runs through the early dialogues. It teaches you how little you know about words you use constantly.
variations: Define a word with a friend.
Pick a word from the news.
Try it on a word you love.

practices.name: Fold a perfect solid
practices.instructions: Fold or cut and glue one of the five regular solids from paper: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron or icosahedron. Print a net or draw your own. Plato in the Timaeus matched four of them to the elements and the fifth to the heavens. Hold it up to the light, and put it where you can see it.
practices.why: The five regular solids are called the Platonic solids because Plato used them in the Timaeus. Making one by hand makes the idea real.
variations: Start with a cube.
Make a set of five.
Hang it as a mobile.

practices.name: Shadows on the wall
practices.instructions: Hold your hand in front of a lamp or the morning sun and look at its shadow on the wall. Move your fingers. Ask what the shadow tells you about the hand and what it leaves out. This is the cave from the Republic: prisoners who mistake shadows for the real. Then ask: what shadows am I taking for the real today?
practices.why: The allegory of the cave is the most famous image in philosophy. Playing with real shadows makes it vivid.
variations: Make shadow animals with a child.
Watch your shadow lengthen.
Write the shadow you suspect.

practices.name: A dialogue with myself
practices.instructions: Write a short dialogue between you and an imaginary Socrates about one thing you believe. Let him ask simple questions, such as what do you mean by that? and how do you know? Answer honestly. Keep going for ten lines. Plato invented the philosophical dialogue, and writing one is the best way to find out what you think.
practices.why: Plato wrote all his philosophy as dialogues, and wrote himself out of them. Writing one is a practical way to test your beliefs.
variations: Do it with a real friend as Socrates.
Argue a position you reject.
Write one with a child and let them ask the questions.

practices.name: A plain breakfast
practices.instructions: Eat a plain breakfast of barley or oats, a few olives, a fig or two and water. In the Republic, Socrates praises simple food for its health and calm, and warns that luxury makes both the city and the soul feverish. Notice how it feels to eat what you need, slowly, and what you do not miss.
practices.why: Plato’s ideal diet is simple, and praised for leaving the mind clear. A plain breakfast is a pleasant experiment.
variations: Add honey.
Eat with a friend.
Do it for a week.

practices.name: Music and gymnastic
practices.instructions: Train the body for twenty minutes: run, wrestle, lift, swim, or walk hard. Keep it plain and stop short of exhaustion. Then spend ten minutes on music in Plato’s wide sense. Sing, play, or learn eight lines of good poetry by heart. The rule of this Onda is to train body and soul together.
practices.why: Plato’s education pairs gymnastic and music, the body and the soul, so that neither is neglected. A short session of each is a balanced afternoon.
variations: Learn a poem on the walk.
Play an instrument after exercise.
Do both with a friend.

practices.name: The ladder of beauty
practices.instructions: Find one beautiful thing in front of you: a face, a tree, a well-made tool. Look at it for two full minutes. Then climb, one step at a time. What do all beautiful bodies share with it? What is beautiful in a person’s character, a law, a piece of knowledge? What is beauty itself? Write where you stop climbing.
practices.why: In the Symposium, Diotima describes a ladder of love rising from one beautiful body to beauty itself. Climbing it in thought is a lovely exercise.
variations: Start from a piece of music.
Start from a building.
Start from a friend’s kindness.

practices.name: Walk and talk
practices.instructions: Walk with a friend for half an hour with one question to pursue, such as is it better to suffer wrong than to do it? Do not sit. Take turns to speak and to listen. Plato’s Academy had a grove with covered walks, and Aristotle’s school got its name from walking. Fresh air makes the mind move.
practices.why: Walking and talking is a classic way of doing philosophy in the Academy and the Lyceum. Movement helps thought.
variations: Walk alone and talk to yourself.
Walk by phone with a faraway friend.
Walk a path in a park.

practices.name: I do not know
practices.instructions: Today, when you do not know something, say so plainly: I do not know. Say it at least once in a meeting or conversation where you would normally bluff. Then add: but I would like to find out. Socrates’s wisdom, he says in the Apology, is that he does not think he knows what he does not know. The rule of this Onda is to say I do not know when you do not.
practices.why: Admitting ignorance is the first step of Socratic philosophy. It keeps you honest and opens the way to learning.
variations: Say it to a child.
Say it before looking something up.
Say it about an opinion.

practices.name: Teach by question
practices.instructions: For the next twenty minutes, in a conversation or lesson, ask questions only and offer no statements. Ask what do you mean, why do you think so and what would follow if you were right? Be curious and kind. Notice how the other person thinks it through for themselves. Socrates charged no fees and gave no lectures.
practices.why: The Socratic method is teaching by questions, drawing out what the learner already half knows. It is a respectful and powerful way to talk.
variations: Use it on a child.
Use it in a team meeting.
Use it on yourself.

practices.name: Follow the argument
practices.instructions: Choose a belief of yours and argue it to the end, step by step, writing each step down. If you reach a conclusion you dislike, do not look away: ask which step is wrong. If no step is wrong, accept it. The rule of this Onda is to follow the argument wherever it leads. Note whether you changed your mind.
practices.why: Following the argument wherever it leads is Socrates’s motto in the Republic. It takes courage to follow it.
variations: Do it with a friend as an opponent.
Do it on a political issue.
Do it on a personal choice.

practices.name: The charioteer’s review
practices.instructions: Go back over the day and sort its moments by which part of you was in charge. When did appetite pull: food, comfort, money, the screen? When did spirit pull: anger, pride, the wish to win, shame? When did reason hold the reins? Write three lines. Plan one small way to let reason drive tomorrow. Think of the soul as a charioteer with two horses.
practices.why: In the Phaedrus, Plato compares the soul to a charioteer driving a white horse of spirit and a dark horse of appetite. The review turns the image into a daily practice.
variations: Name the horses by what they wanted.
Draw the chariot.
Review only one hour.

practices.name: A little symposium
practices.instructions: Hold a mini-symposium at the end of dinner. Choose one question, such as what is love? or is it good to be rich? Each person speaks in turn, with no interrupting, and the host closes with questions. Drink water or watered juice in the Greek style. Share dried figs and nuts. Plato’s Symposium gives each guest a speech about love; the best comes from Socrates.
practices.why: The symposium was the Greek after-dinner drinking party, where the best talk happened. A sober version keeps the talk and drops the hangover.
variations: Agree to speak in praise of something.
Use Plato’s question about love.
End with a toast to the host.

practices.name: Read the Apology aloud
practices.instructions: Read part of Plato’s Apology aloud, Socrates’s speech at his trial. Choose the passage where he says the unexamined life is not worth living, or where he says he is wiser only because he knows he knows nothing. Read it slowly, with the pauses. Imagine the room. Sit quietly after.
practices.why: The Apology is the best introduction to Socrates, and reads well aloud. Its courage and humour are unforgettable.
variations: Read it with a friend, taking turns.
Listen to a recording.
Read the final speech.

practices.name: Look up at the cosmos
practices.instructions: Go outdoors after dark and look at the sky for fifteen minutes. Plato called the world a kosmos, an ordered beauty, and thought the circling stars were the visible image of an eternal order. Find the moon or a planet and watch for movement. Ask what order lies behind what you see.
practices.why: In the Timaeus, Plato describes the heavens as a moving image of eternity. Stargazing is the oldest form of wonder.
variations: Find the pole star.
Learn one constellation.
Sketch the sky.

practices.name: Return to the cave
practices.instructions: Tell someone what you learned today, or one thing that you now see differently. In the Republic, the freed prisoner must go back into the cave and tell the others what he has seen. Do it with kindness and without scorn. Notice how hard it is to explain, and how much you learn by trying.
practices.why: The return to the cave is the philosopher’s duty to share what has been seen. Explaining something to a friend is the best test of understanding.
variations: Explain it to a child.
Write it as a letter.
Ask the listener to repeat it back.

practices.name: A question for tomorrow
practices.instructions: Before bed, write one question that you want to work on tomorrow. Make it clear and open: what is a good friend? How should I spend my time? Leave it by the bed. Plato says that philosophy begins in wonder. Let the night work on the question and see whether the morning has something to say.
practices.why: Philosophy begins in wonder, as Socrates tells Theaetetus. A written question gives the sleeping mind a task.
variations: Ask a question about a person.
Ask a question about a choice.
Ask the question you are afraid of.

practices.name: A day in the Academy
practices.instructions: Spend a morning as in Plato’s Academy: begin with a geometry problem, walk with a friend discussing one question, read a page of a dialogue aloud, and end with a plain meal of bread, olives and fruit. Keep a list of the questions you asked. The Academy lasted over 900 years, so you are in good company.
practices.why: Plato’s Academy was a school of mathematics, argument and shared life. A day in its spirit is a retreat for the mind.
variations: Do it with two friends.
Do it in a park with trees.
Finish with a toast of water.

practices.name: A Socratic dinner
practices.instructions: Invite friends to a simple dinner in the Greek style: bread, olives, cheese, figs, boiled greens, chickpeas. Choose a question beforehand, and send it with the invitation. After eating, discuss it, one speech each. Include a toast to someone who is not there. Keep the talk friendly, not competitive, and let the evening run long.
practices.why: The dinner and the talk that follows are the setting of Plato’s Symposium. Recreating it gives friends the gift of a long, structured conversation.
variations: Pick a question about friendship.
Ask everyone to bring a quotation.
Finish by reading the closing page of the Symposium.

immersePlan.name: Read the Apology
immersePlan.text: Read Plato’s account of Socrates at his trial. Read it in one sitting if you can, and note the line that strikes you.

immersePlan.name: Read the Symposium
immersePlan.text: Read a section of Plato’s drinking party where each guest speaks about love. Read Aristophanes’s speech about the split humans.

immersePlan.name: Read the cave in the Republic
immersePlan.text: Read the allegory of the cave at the start of Book VII. Read it slowly and think of your own shadows.

immersePlan.name: Watch Rossellini’s Socrates
immersePlan.text: Watch Roberto Rossellini’s 1971 film of Socrates’s last days. It is slow and thoughtful. Notice the calm.

immersePlan.name: Watch The Matrix
immersePlan.text: Watch the 1999 film in which a man discovers that the world he knows is a simulation. It is the cave retold.

immersePlan.name: Watch My Dinner with Andre
immersePlan.text: Watch Louis Malle’s 1981 film, two men talking at dinner for two hours about life, theatre and being awake. It is a modern symposium.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Satie’s Socrate
immersePlan.text: Play Erik Satie’s 1918 symphonic drama on Plato’s texts, sung with calm, clear lines. Follow the translation of the death scene.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Bernstein’s Serenade
immersePlan.text: Play Leonard Bernstein’s violin concerto in five movements, one for each speaker at Plato’s banquet. Follow along with the titles.

immersePlan.name: Listen to In Our Time on the Republic
immersePlan.text: Play the BBC radio discussion of the Republic by three scholars. Listen while walking.

immersePlan.name: Look at The School of Athens
immersePlan.text: Look at Raphael’s fresco of Plato pointing up and Aristotle pointing out, surrounded by the philosophers. Find Diogenes on the steps.

immersePlan.name: Look at The Death of Socrates
immersePlan.text: Look at Jacques-Louis David’s painting of Socrates reaching for the cup, still teaching. Notice the weeping friends.

immersePlan.name: Look at the five regular solids
immersePlan.text: Look at drawings of the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron, and match each to an element as Plato did.

immersePlan.name: Make maza
immersePlan.text: Knead barley meal with water or oil into a simple cake, the daily bread of the Greeks. Eat it with olives.

immersePlan.name: Eat olives, cheese and figs
immersePlan.text: Make a plate of olives, cheese and figs with boiled greens and chickpeas, the plain fare of the Republic. Eat it slowly.

immersePlan.name: Eat figs and nuts
immersePlan.text: Eat dried figs and nuts at the end of a meal, as the Greek second tables did. Share them while you talk.

immersePlan.name: Drink diluted grape juice
immersePlan.text: Mix grape juice with two or three parts water in a bowl and serve it in cups, in the Greek manner. Use juice rather than wine. Sip it slowly.

immersePlan.name: Drink water from a cup
immersePlan.text: Drink a cup of cool water, slowly, and think about the idea of thirst and its satisfaction. Socrates liked to ask what it is that thirst really wants.

immersePlan.name: Make kykeon
immersePlan.text: Stir barley meal into water with a little honey or mint and drink it. It is the oldest Greek porridge-drink.

immersePlan.name: Hold a symposium
immersePlan.text: Gather friends after a meal for talk on one question, with water in cups. Each speaks in turn.

immersePlan.name: Teach by question
immersePlan.text: In one conversation today, ask only questions: what do you mean, how do you know. See what the other person finds.

immersePlan.name: Walk and talk with a friend
immersePlan.text: Take a friend for a half-hour walk and discuss one question. Do not sit down.

immersePlan.name: Play petteia
immersePlan.text: Play the ancient Greek board game of capture by surrounding. Draw a grid and use pebbles in two colours.

immersePlan.name: Play knucklebones
immersePlan.text: Toss five small stones or dice in the air and catch them on the back of the hand. Play with a friend, and count your catches.

immersePlan.name: Play kottabos with water
immersePlan.text: Flick drops of water from a cup at a target, as Greek drinkers flicked wine lees at a bowl. Use water and a cup, and lay a cloth down.

immersePlan.name: Look up the Panathenaea
immersePlan.text: Read about Athens’s great midsummer festival, with a procession carrying a new robe to the goddess. Plan your own procession to a favourite spot.

immersePlan.name: Keep Plato’s birthday
immersePlan.text: Plato’s birthday is kept on 7 November, as it was by his followers for centuries. Share a meal and one question with a friend.

immersePlan.name: Look up Plato’s Academy
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the olive grove in Athens where Plato taught. Imagine walking between its trees.

immersePlan.name: Practise aporia
immersePlan.text: Aporia is the state of being at a loss. Find one question that leaves you at a loss and stay with it without rushing to an answer.

immersePlan.name: Practise elenchos
immersePlan.text: Elenchos is examination by questioning. Examine one of your own beliefs with three questions before bed.

immersePlan.name: Practise arete
immersePlan.text: Arete means excellence. Do one task today in the way that shows its excellence, however humble.

rules.why: Take a thing you are sure of and ask what exactly it means and how you know it.

rules.text: Say I do not know when you do not
rules.why: Pretended knowledge blocks the way to the real thing.
Go where the reasoning leads, even when it is against your side or your comfort.
Appetite and anger are to be heard, and then steered. They do not drive.
Exercise and music every day, so that you grow neither brutal nor soft.

rules.text: Prefer the real to the seeming
rules.why: Care more about being good than about looking good.

read.title: Apology
read.creator: Plato
read.why: Socrates’ defence at his trial. Short, proud and the best place to begin.

read.title: Symposium
read.creator: Plato
read.why: Seven speeches about love at a drinking party, ending with the ladder of beauty and a drunken Alcibiades. The most enjoyable dialogue.

read.title: Republic
read.creator: Plato
read.why: What is justice, and is the just person happier? The answer takes ten books, an imaginary city, the sun, the line and the cave.

read.title: Phaedo
read.creator: Plato
read.why: The last day of Socrates, spent arguing in his cell that the soul does not die.

read.title: The Sovereignty of Good
read.creator: Iris Murdoch
read.why: Three essays by a novelist and philosopher who makes Plato’s idea of the Good usable in ordinary moral life.

read.title: The Last Days of Socrates
read.creator: Plato, trans. Hugh Tredennick and Harold Tarrant
read.why: Euthyphro, Apology, Crito and Phaedo in one small book.

watch.title: Socrates
watch.creator: Roberto Rossellini
watch.why: A plain, careful film for television that stages the trial and death almost entirely in Plato’s words.

watch.title: The Matrix
watch.creator: Lana and Lilly Wachowski
watch.why: The cave retold: prisoners who take a projection for the world, and one who is turned round.

watch.title: My Dinner with Andre
watch.creator: Louis Malle
watch.why: Two men talk through a meal about how to live. The nearest thing on film to a dialogue.

listen.title: Socrate
listen.creator: Erik Satie
listen.why: Passages of Plato on Socrates set for voice and small orchestra, as white and even as an antique frieze. It ends with the death in the Phaedo.

listen.title: Serenade after Plato’s Symposium
listen.creator: Leonard Bernstein
listen.why: A violin concerto in five movements, each named after speakers at the banquet.

listen.title: Music of Ancient Greece
listen.creator: Atrium Musicae de Madrid, directed by Gregorio Paniagua
listen.why: Reconstructions of the surviving fragments, including the Delphic hymns. A guess at how the modes sounded that Plato wanted to regulate.

listen.title: Plato’s Republic
listen.creator: In Our Time, BBC Radio 4
listen.why: Three scholars talk through the book in forty-five minutes.

art.title: The School of Athens
art.creator: Raphael
art.why: A fresco in the Vatican. Plato, with the face of Leonardo, points to the sky and carries the Timaeus. Aristotle beside him holds his hand flat over the earth.

art.title: The Death of Socrates
art.creator: Jacques-Louis David
art.why: Socrates reaches for the cup while still teaching. Plato sits at the foot of the bed, an old man, though he was young at the time and was not there. In the Metropolitan Museum, New York.

art.title: Plato’s Academy mosaic
art.creator: Roman workshop, from a villa near Pompeii
art.why: Seven philosophers gathered under a tree round a globe. In the National Archaeological Museum, Naples.

art.title: The five regular solids
art.creator: Described in the Timaeus
art.why: Tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron. Plato assigned them to fire, earth, air, the cosmos and water.

eat.title: Maza
eat.creator: Barley meal kneaded with water or oil into a flat cake
eat.why: The daily bread of Athens. The first, healthy city of the Republic lives on it, served on clean leaves.

eat.title: Olives, cheese and figs
eat.creator: With boiled greens and chickpeas
eat.why: The relishes Socrates allows his simple citizens when Glaucon complains that he is feeding them like pigs.

eat.title: Dried figs and nuts
eat.creator: The second tables
eat.why: At a symposium the tables were cleared and brought back with fruit and nuts for the drinking and the talk.

drink.title: Wine mixed with water
drink.creator: Two or three parts water to one of wine
drink.why: Greeks thought unmixed wine barbarous. The leader of the symposium set the strength for all.

drink.title: Water
drink.creator: From a cup or a spring
drink.why: Socrates could drink anyone under the table and was never seen drunk. He was as content with water.

drink.title: Kykeon
drink.creator: Barley and water, sometimes with mint or cheese
drink.why: A thick country drink mentioned in the Republic as a soldier’s and a farmer’s refreshment.

customs.title: The symposium
customs.creator: Drinking together after dinner
customs.why: Guests reclined on couches, poured a libation, agreed how much to drink and took turns to speak or sing.

customs.title: Teaching by question
customs.creator: No lectures, no fees
customs.why: Socrates took no money and claimed to teach nothing. He questioned people in the marketplace, the gymnasium and the workshops.

customs.title: Walking and talking
customs.creator: In the grove and the colonnade
customs.why: Philosophy was done on foot and in company. The Phaedrus takes place on a walk along a stream outside the walls.

customs.title: Philosophy written as conversation
customs.creator: The dialogue
customs.why: Plato never speaks in his own voice. Each dialogue is a scene with named people, and the reader has to judge the argument for themselves.

games.title: Petteia
games.creator: Board game · Greece
games.why: A game of pebbles on a grid in which a piece is captured by being trapped between two others. Plato uses it as an image for dialectic.

games.title: Knucklebones
games.creator: Game of skill and chance · Greece
games.why: Played with the ankle bones of sheep, thrown as dice or tossed and caught. Boys are playing it when Socrates arrives in the Lysis.

games.title: Wrestling
games.creator: Sport · Greece
games.why: The centre of gymnastic education. Plato is said to have wrestled at the Isthmian Games, and his name may be a nickname meaning broad.

games.title: Kottabos
games.creator: Drinking game · Greece
games.why: At a symposium, players flicked the dregs of their wine at a target across the room.

festivals.title: The Panathenaea
festivals.creator: Midsummer, in the Athenian month Hekatombaion
festivals.why: The great festival of Athena, with a procession to the Acropolis, games and recitations of Homer. Several dialogues are set during it.

festivals.title: The Bendideia
festivals.creator: Early summer, in the month Thargelion
festivals.why: A festival of the Thracian goddess Bendis at the port of Piraeus, with a torch race on horseback. Socrates has gone down to see it when the Republic begins.

festivals.title: Plato’s birthday
festivals.creator: 7 Thargelion; kept on 7 November since the Renaissance
festivals.why: Ancient Platonists held a banquet with readings each year. Marsilio Ficino revived it in Florence in the 1460s with a reading of the Symposium.

places.title: Plato’s Academy
places.creator: Akadimia Platonos, Athens, Greece
places.why: A quiet public park a short way north-west of the centre, with the foundations of the gymnasium among the trees and a small digital museum nearby.

places.title: The Ancient Agora
places.creator: Athens, Greece
places.why: The marketplace where Socrates questioned people. The foundations of a building thought to be the prison where he died lie just outside it.

places.title: Ortygia
places.creator: Syracuse, Sicily, Italy
places.why: The island citadel of the tyrants Plato tried three times to educate. The Greek theatre and quarries are on the mainland opposite.

places.title: The Stanza della Segnatura
places.creator: Vatican Museums, Vatican City
places.why: The room that holds the School of Athens. Go early, and bring a list of who is who.

places.title: Villa Medici at Careggi
places.creator: Florence, Italy
places.why: Where Ficino translated Plato for Cosimo de’ Medici and the Florentine circle met. Check whether it is open before you travel.

ethics.title: Wisdom
ethics.text: The rule of reason in the soul: knowing what is good for the whole of oneself and not only for one part.
ethics.practice: Before one decision today, ask what each part of you wants and what is good for all of you.

ethics.title: Courage
ethics.text: Keeping hold, through pain and pleasure, of the right belief about what is truly to be feared.
ethics.practice: Do one thing you have been putting off out of fear.

ethics.title: Moderation
ethics.text: Agreement among the parts of the soul that the better should lead. It shows as ease, and it is not the same as strain.
ethics.practice: Stop one pleasure today while you still want more.

ethics.title: Justice
ethics.text: Each part doing its own work. The just person is at peace within and therefore deals fairly outside.
ethics.practice: Notice one place where you are meddling in what is not your business, and step back.

ethics.title: Better to suffer wrong than to do it
ethics.text: Doing injustice damages the soul of the one who does it. That is a worse harm than anything suffered.
ethics.practice: Think of a wrong you got away with. What did it cost you?

ethics.title: Care of the soul
ethics.text: Socrates told Athens to care less for money and reputation and more for the state of its soul.
ethics.practice: Count the minutes you gave today to each of the three.

philosophy.title: The Forms
philosophy.text: Behind the many changing beautiful, equal or just things there is in each case one thing that is perfectly and always so. It is grasped by thought and not by the senses.
philosophy.practice: Find two things you call fair and ask what makes both of them so.

philosophy.title: The cave
philosophy.text: We are like prisoners who have only ever seen shadows on a wall. Education is being turned round, dragged up into the daylight, and then going back down to help.
philosophy.practice: Name one shadow you have mistaken for the thing itself.

philosophy.title: The Good as the sun
philosophy.text: As the sun gives things both their visibility and their growth, the Good makes everything else intelligible and worth pursuing.
philosophy.practice: Ask of your main aim this year: good for what?

philosophy.title: The divided line
philosophy.text: There are grades of clarity: images, things, mathematical reasoning and direct understanding. Most of life is spent on the lower half.
philosophy.practice: Take one belief and place it on the line.

philosophy.title: The three-part soul
philosophy.text: Reason, spirit and appetite. Inner conflict is real, and a good life is one where the three are friends.
philosophy.practice: Catch one inner argument today and identify the speakers.

philosophy.title: Recollection
philosophy.text: We could not look for what we did not in some way already know. Learning draws out what is latent.
philosophy.practice: Teach someone something today using questions only.

philosophy.title: Love as ascent
philosophy.text: Desire is not to be killed. It is to be educated, from the love of one body upwards to the love of what is beautiful in itself.
philosophy.practice: Ask what your strongest desire is really a desire for.

philosophy.title: Knowing that you do not know
philosophy.text: The oracle called Socrates the wisest of men. He concluded it was because he alone did not think he knew what he did not.
philosophy.practice: List three things you act as if you know.

journal: What did you find you did not know?
Which shadow did you take for the real thing?
Which part of your soul drove today?
What question did you avoid asking?
Where did you follow the argument, and where did you leave it?
What word do you use without being able to define it?
What was beautiful today, and why?
Did you care more about being good or about seeming good?
What did you do for your body, and what for your soul?
Whom did you really talk with?

What would you do with a ring that made you invisible?
What did appetite ask for?
What made you angry, and was the anger on the side of reason?
What are you in love with, and where is it leading you?
When were you at a loss, and did you stay there?
What do you believe on someone else’s authority?
Who turned you round, and when?
What would you go back down into the cave for?
What is your own work, and did you do it?
What did you teach, and how?

What did a daily proof do to your thinking?
Which horse do you know better now?

Where did you glimpse something that does not change?
Which question will you keep asking?

intro: Plato was born in Athens around 427 BCE into one of its oldest families, at the start of a long war that the city would lose. He was expected to go into politics. What changed his course was an ugly, barefoot stonemason’s son named Socrates, who spent his days in the marketplace asking people what they meant by courage, or piety, or justice, and showing them that they could not say.

In 399 BCE the restored democracy tried Socrates for impiety and for corrupting the young, and put him to death. Plato was about twenty-eight. He left Athens for some years, and when he came back he did two things that shaped the rest of Western thought. He began to write dialogues, philosophical dramas in which Socrates is usually the main speaker. And in about 387 he founded a school in a grove sacred to the hero Akademos, where mathematics, astronomy and philosophy were studied by men and at least two women for the love of it. Aristotle stayed there for twenty years.

The early dialogues show Socrates at work: testing, refuting, professing ignorance. In the middle ones a positive picture appears. The things we see and touch are always changing and are never perfectly what we call them. No drawn circle is truly round. Yet we know what a circle is. So there must be, Plato reasons, a perfect and unchanging Circle, Justice and Beauty that our minds grasp and that visible things only resemble. He calls these Forms. At their head stands the Good, which is to thought what the sun is to sight.

From this follows a view of human life. The soul belongs with the Forms more than with the body. It has three parts, reason, spirit and appetite, and it is healthy when reason rules with the consent of the others. Education is the turning of the whole soul from shadows towards what is real, as in the famous image of the cave. Love, rightly led, climbs from one beautiful body to Beauty itself. And a city will not be well governed until those who rule it are those who love wisdom and do not want power.

Plato went three times to Syracuse to try this last idea on a real ruler, and failed each time. His late works are more cautious, and he criticises his own theory of Forms sharply. He died at about eighty, by one account at a wedding feast. His writings survive complete, which is true of no other major ancient philosopher.

This Onda takes the Academy’s day as its pattern: a proof in the morning, a definition tested by questions, exercise and music, the contemplation of something beautiful and an evening review of who held the reins. You will not be asked to believe in the Forms. You will be asked to notice how much of what you say you know is only opinion, and to find that this is a beginning.
guide.origin: Athens, in a grove outside the Dipylon gate
guide.era: Plato lived from about 427 to 347 BCE. His Academy lasted in one form or another for nine centuries

figures.name: Socrates
figures.bio: Plato’s teacher. He wrote nothing, claimed to know nothing and was executed by Athens. Almost all we know of him comes from Plato and Xenophon.

figures.name: Plato
figures.bio: Founder of the Academy and author of some thirty dialogues. His given name was reportedly Aristocles.

figures.name: Diotima of Mantinea
figures.bio: The priestess who, Socrates says in the Symposium, taught him everything he knew about love. She may be Plato’s invention.

figures.name: Aristotle
figures.bio: Plato’s greatest pupil and sharpest critic. He rejected separate Forms and founded his own school, the Lyceum.

figures.name: Speusippus
figures.bio: Plato’s nephew and his successor as head of the Academy.

figures.name: Axiothea of Phlius
figures.bio: One of two women recorded as students at the Academy. She is said to have come after reading the Republic, and to have dressed as a man.

figures.name: Plotinus
figures.bio: The founder of what is now called Neoplatonism. He taught in Rome that all things flow from the One and long to return to it.

figures.name: Hypatia
figures.bio: Mathematician and head of the Platonist school at Alexandria. She was murdered by a Christian mob.

figures.name: Augustine of Hippo
figures.bio: The Christian bishop who said the books of the Platonists prepared him for conversion, and who carried much of Plato into Christian theology.

figures.name: Marsilio Ficino
figures.bio: Florentine priest and physician who made the first complete Latin translation of Plato, published in 1484, and coined the phrase Platonic love.

history.detail: In Athens or on Aegina, four years into the Peloponnesian War. On his mother’s side he descends from the lawgiver Solon.
After Athens surrenders to Sparta a junta of thirty takes power. It includes two of Plato’s relatives and kills some fifteen hundred citizens. Plato is repelled.
Convicted by a jury of 501, he refuses to propose exile, refuses to escape, and drinks hemlock a month later.
Plato visits the Pythagoreans of southern Italy and the court of Dionysius I at Syracuse. On his return he founds the school.
Invited by Dion to educate the young Dionysius II, Plato sails for Syracuse. Court intrigue wrecks the plan. The seventeen-year-old Aristotle joins the Academy.
Plato returns to Syracuse, is held under guard and is extracted by friends. The Seventh Letter, if genuine, is his account of the affair.
He is buried in the grounds of the Academy. He leaves the Laws unfinished.
Under Arcesilaus the school turns to Socratic doubt and argues for two centuries that nothing can be known for certain.
The Roman general besieges the city and fells the trees of the Academy for siege engines. Platonists continue to teach elsewhere.
In Rome he builds a spiritual system on Plato. His pupil Porphyry edits it as the Enneads.
The emperor Justinian forbids pagans to teach. The last Platonists of Athens leave for Persia.
Cosimo de’ Medici gives Ficino a Greek manuscript and a villa. The Latin Plato is printed in Florence in 1484.
Henri Estienne prints the Greek text in Geneva. Its page numbers and letters are still used to cite Plato.

concepts.detail: Perfect, unchanging objects of knowledge, such as Beauty, Equality and Justice, of which visible things are imperfect likenesses. Plato himself raised the hardest objections to the theory in the Parmenides.
The highest object of study. Socrates says he cannot define it and offers the sun as its child and likeness.
Prisoners chained from birth watch shadows cast by a fire. One is freed, climbs out, is dazzled, comes to see the sun, and returns to those who will not believe him.
Argued in Republic 4 from the fact of inner conflict. Each part has its own desires, and each has a virtue.
Offered in the Meno and Phaedo as the answer to how we can seek what we do not know, and as evidence that the soul existed before birth.
Disciplined conversation that tests assumptions and rises towards an unassumed first principle. In the Republic it comes only after ten years of mathematics.
A spirit between mortal and divine, the child of Resource and Poverty, always lacking and always seeking. Properly led, it is philosophy itself.

concepts.text: Power for those who do not want it.
concepts.detail: The proposal that cities be governed by people trained for decades to know the Good, owning no property and ruling as a duty.
Coined by Ficino for a love between friends that leads both towards the divine. Its modern meaning of love without sex is narrower than Plato’s own account.

facts.text: Plato mentions himself only three times in the dialogues: twice as present at the trial of Socrates, and once as absent, ill, from his death.
Every work Plato is known to have published has survived, along with several he probably did not write.
The numbers and letters used to cite Plato, such as Republic 514a, are the pages and sections of a Geneva edition of 1578.
The Academy held its land for the worship of the Muses, which made it legally a religious association.
The Republic proposes that women of the ruling class receive the same education and hold the same offices as men.
The story of Atlantis first appears in Plato’s Timaeus and Critias, and nowhere earlier.

sensitivity.note: Plato wrote dialogues, not doctrine, and scholars disagree about how much of what Socrates says in them Plato himself believed. This Onda borrows his exercises and questions. It does not ask you to accept his politics or his metaphysics.
requiredCaveats: The ideal city of the Republic censors poets, deceives its citizens and abolishes the family for its rulers. Many readers have found it authoritarian.
Athens ran on slavery and excluded women from public life. Plato questions the second and largely accepts the first.
